Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

civil adjective

of citizens, not military or of the church

also civil war, civil law, civil rights, civilian, civic, loss of civil rights, deprive of civil rights

classical

Cic. Att. 7.13.1: ita cīvīle est
Traupman 178, 194
Traupman 291

cīvīlis, cīvīle

Declension on Wiktionary

of citizens, civil

Of citizens among themselves: bellum cīvīle, civil war (Cic.; Caesar’s Bellum cīvīle); jūs cīvīle, the civil law, the private law of Roman citizens (Lewis & Short); civil rights are jūra cīvīlia (Traupman 194) or jūs cīvīle (Traupman 178). Civil as against military: nōn mīlitāribus sōlum sed cīvīlibus quoque mūneribus (Liv. 9.3.5, Lewis & Short). It also means political (see political), and from Augustus on, of a great man, affable, behaving as one citizen among others (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • togātus, togāta, togātum — civilian, in civilian dress

    also used · classical · Cic. Sull. 85: cui ūnī togātō supplicātiōnem dēcrēverit (Lewis & Short); Traupman 178; Traupman 291 · Declension on Wiktionary

    Wearing the toga, the citizen’s dress in peace, and so as a noun a civilian, against a soldier: Cicero is the only civilian for whom the senate decreed a thanksgiving (Lewis & Short). Traupman gives togātus and prīvātus for civilian.

  • intestīnus, intestīna, intestīnum — internal, within the state

    also used · classical · Cic. Cat. 2.28: bellum intestīnum (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. civil war · Declension on Wiktionary

    Inward, internal; with bellum, a war within the state, and Morgan–Owens’s first word for civil war (after Milton). As a noun, intestīna are the guts.

  • jūs cīvīle — the civil law

    also used · classical · Traupman 178: civil rights

    Classically the law of the citizens, the civil law; Traupman gives it for “civil rights”, which classical Latin would express otherwise.

Examples

  • genus bellī quod sit vidēs. ita cīvīle est ut nōn ex cīvium dissēnsiōne sed ex ūnīus perditī cīvis audāciā nātum sit.

    you see what kind of war it is: civil, but born not of a quarrel among citizens but of the reckless daring of one desperate citizen.Cic. Att. 7.13.1

  • capitis dēminūtiō

    loss of civil rightsTraupman 178

  • jūs cīvīle

    civil law (Traupman: civil rights)Traupman 291

  • aliquem capite dēminuere

    to deprive someone of civil rightsTraupman 291

  • dēminūtiō capitis

    loss of civil rights, loss of civil statusTraupman 291

See also political, citizen, civil servant, polite.
